Introduction

St. Catherine, called Katherine on the cited page, is commemorated as a learned martyr of Alexandria. The OCA life recounts her education, confession before imperial authorities, and the tradition of her relics at Sinai. It explicitly notes November 25 in Greek usage, while its own entry is November 24. Narrative and miraculous details remain attributed to the published hagiographic source.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The Orthodox life places St. Catherine in Alexandria, educated in philosophy, medicine, and rhetoric. It recounts an elder’s instruction and her vision of Christ.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life, body paragraph 1; opening: The Holy Great Martyr Katherine was the daughter of Konstos,…

Clugnet’s historical Roman Catholic article retells her Acts below and then discusses their later, elaborated textual forms. The quoted episodes belong to that hagiographic narrative.

[2] Historical reference article · Article, narrative and following textual discussion

Life and notable events

Of noble birth and learned in the sciences, when only eighteen years old, Catherine presented herself to the Emperor Maximinus who was violently persecuting the Christians, upbraided him for his cruelty and endeavoured to prove how iniquitous was the worship of false gods. Astounded at the young girl's audacity, but incompetent to vie with her in point of learning the tyrant detained her in his palace and summoned numerous scholars whom he commanded to use all their skill in specious reasoning that thereby Catherine might be led to apostatize. But she emerged from the debate victorious. Several of her adversaries, conquered by her eloquence, declared themselves Christians and were at once put to death.

[2] Historical reference article · Article, narrative of the Acts; education and disputation

Death and martyrdom

Furious at being baffled, Maximinus had Catherine scourged and then imprisoned. Meanwhile the empress, eager to see so extraordinary a young woman, went with Porphyry, the head of the troops, to visit her in her dungeon, when they in turn yielded to Catherine's exhortations, believed, were baptized, and immediately won the martyr's crown. Soon afterwards the saint, who far from forsaking her Faith, effected so many conversions, was condemned to die on the wheel, but, at her touch, this instrument of torture was miraculously destroyed. The emperor, enraged beyond control, then had her beheaded and angels carried her body to Mount Sinai where later a church and monastery were built in her honour. So far the Acts of St. Catherine.

[2] Historical reference article · Article, narrative of the Acts; prison visitors, wheel, beheading, and Sinai

The Orthodox life also describes the empress, Porphyrios, and soldiers confessing Christ and dying before St. Catherine’s final beheading.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life: prison visitors and fellow martyrs

Writings and legacy

The spiked wheel having become emblematic of the saint, wheelwrights and mechanics placed themselves under her patronage. Finally, as according to tradition, she not only remained a virgin by governing her passions and conquered her executioners by wearying their patience, but triumphed in science by closing the mouths of sophists, her intercession was implored by theologians, apologists, pulpit orators, and philosophers. Before studying, writing, or preaching, they besought her to illumine their minds, guide their pens, and impart eloquence to their words.

[2] Historical reference article · Article, iconographic wheel and later Western patronage

Her relics and monastery are associated with Sinai. The source notes November 25 in Greek usage.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life: Sinai and calendar note

Source context and historical limits

The identified source is a modern ecclesiastical life used in the Church’s commemoration. It transmits biographical material, received traditions, and—in some accounts—miracle narratives. Those claims remain attributed to this source; this app has not independently established a critical historical chronology or verified each miraculous episode. The source also notes November 25 in Greek usage; November 24 follows this OCA entry.
